sources.note: Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-17. Quoted: 'Most problems with outbound connectivity ... is due to SNAT port exhaustion'; 'Default port allocation ... isn't a recommended method'; 'For most scenarios, Azure recommends using a NAT gateway for outbound connectivity ... highly recommended if your service is initiating repeated TCP or UDP outbound connections to the same destination'; 'a NAT gateway dynamically allocates SNAT ports across all VM instances within a subnet'; 'assigning individual public IP addresses isn't a scalable solution'; 'aggressive or brute force retries without decay and back-off logic cause exhaustion to occur or persist'. The metric names and that a NAT gateway takes over a subnet's outbound traffic from load balancer outbound rules are from memory (to verify).

brief.situation: You are the network engineer at Haldane Freight. The label service (12 VMs in snet-labels, behind a Standard internal load balancer, outbound through the public load balancer's default port allocation) calls the carrier's single label API. Since the afternoon wave started, 15% of label requests time out. The carrier's pickup cut-off is 17:00: any parcel without a label misses today's truck.
handover: The carrier allowlists our egress IPs; adding one takes them 15 minutes after a ticket.
The label client retries immediately, up to five times, on a timeout.
howItWorks: The terminal shows each command's output; the diagram shows the label VMs, the load balancer's outbound SNAT ports and the carrier API they all call.
Each command takes a minute or two; the clock moves only when you act or wait.
When you close, you write the record and explain your reasoning.

natgw.label: Get the carrier to allowlist two new public IPs, then attach NAT gateway ng-labels (those 2 IPs) to snet-labels
natgw.available: not busy and (not fixed and not harmed)
natgw.why: Already done, or the system is down.

effects.output:
neteng@cloudshell:~$ (carrier ticket CR-88120: allowlist 20.84.30.11 and 20.84.30.12; confirmed 15:5x)
neteng@cloudshell:~$ az network nat gateway create -g rg-labels -n ng-labels --public-ip-addresses pip-ng-1 pip-ng-2 --idle-timeout 4
neteng@cloudshell:~$ az network vnet subnet update -g rg-labels --vnet-name vnet-ops -n snet-labels --nat-gateway ng-labels

effects.log: The subnet's outbound traffic now uses the NAT gateway, which allocates ports on demand across all VMs from two IPs, instead of 1,024 fixed ports per VM; the carrier accepts the new IPs because they were allowlisted first.

reuse.label: Enable keep-alive and connection pooling in the label client, add back-off to retries, and alert on SNAT failures
reuse.available: not busy and (not planned and not harmed)
reuse.why: Already done, or the system is down.

effects.output:
neteng@cloudshell:~$ git diff src/carrier/client.ts
-  keepAlive: false
+  keepAlive: true, maxSockets: 64
-  retries: 5, backoff: none
+  retries: 3, backoff: exponential with jitter
neteng@cloudshell:~$ az monitor metrics alert create -n ng-labels-snat --condition 'total SNATConnectionCount where ConnectionState == Failed > 0' ...

effects.log: Fewer, reused connections need far fewer ports, retries no longer pile on, and any SNAT failure alerts.

writeup.question: For the record: why label calls timed out, what you changed in what order, and what reduces port use.

parts.label: Why
parts.modelAnswer: Each VM had used all 1,024 default SNAT ports and failed SNAT connections began with the wave; ss showed hundreds of short connections to one carrier IP, and the client opened a new connection per request and retried immediately.

parts.label: Changed
parts.modelAnswer: The carrier allowlisted two new IPs first; then NAT gateway ng-labels with those IPs on snet-labels. Per-VM public IPs would have exposed the VMs and been refused by the carrier; restarts only freed ports briefly.

parts.label: Port use
parts.modelAnswer: Keep-alive with a pool and exponential back-off with jitter cut the connections needed; an alert fires on any SNAT failure.

exposedVms.headline: Scale outbound with a NAT gateway
exposedVms.body: Per-VM public IPs do not scale and widen exposure. A NAT gateway with allowlisted IPs gives the subnet ports on demand.

truckMissed.headline: Default allocation runs out
truckMissed.body: Default outbound allocation gives each VM a fixed small share of ports. Many connections to one destination exhaust it; a NAT gateway allocates dynamically.

natted.headline: Good: the outbound path that fits the workload
natted.body: You read the SNAT metrics and the connection pattern, had the new IPs allowlisted first, attached a NAT gateway, checked labels, and fixed the client behavior that drove exhaustion.

scoring.modelReasoning: The load balancer shows every VM using all its default SNAT ports, and the VMs open hundreds of short connections to one carrier endpoint with immediate retries. Have the carrier allowlist new IPs, then attach a NAT gateway to the subnet: it allocates ports dynamically across the VMs. Per-VM public IPs expose the VMs and are not allowlisted; restarts free ports only briefly. Then make the client reuse connections and back off, and alert on SNAT failures.
